lead: An IoT service is built by many firms, not one. Chips, devices, connectivity, platforms, apps and integration each add a piece of value. The IoT value chain maps these roles in order. The market perspective asks a second question: which role earns the money, and which business model charges the customer? This matters when a smart-meter project, a fleet tracker or a factory sensor system is priced, bought and scaled. A firm that only counts hardware misses the recurring revenue in connectivity, data and services.
prereq: You need: 1.1 for what IoT is, 1.7 for the M2M comparison, and 1.8 for business issues.

sections.h3: M2M value chains and IoT value chains

blocks.text: An M2M value chain links a device maker, a connectivity supplier, an integrator and an end user. The flow is mostly one-way: a machine sends readings to a monitoring centre. The chain is vertical and hardware-led; value is counted in devices, SIM cards and integration labour. Chapter 1.7 contrasts this with IoT.

An IoT value chain is longer and more layered. Component and chip makers supply sensors, microcontrollers and radios. Device makers turn them into meters, tags, cameras and boards. Network operators supply SIMs, NB-IoT, LoRaWAN or Wi-Fi backhaul. Platform providers run device registries, message brokers, storage and dashboards. System integrators assemble these parts for a customer. Application and service providers build the user-facing service: a phone app, an alert, a billing rule. End users receive the value: a lower bill, a safe plant, a timely repair.

A firm may occupy one role or several. A large company can make chips, devices and a platform. What matters is that each role adds a distinct capability, and no single role owns the whole service. Some syllabi call this layered arrangement the emerging industrial structure.

Market analysis asks which customer segment buys, what it pays for, and who captures the margin. Common segments are consumer (smart home), enterprise (fleet, retail), industrial (factory, energy) and public (water, street lighting). A hospital, a city and a household buy differently: one wants compliance, one wants uptime, one wants low price.

Business models include one-time sale of a device, subscription (₹ per device per month), pay-per-use (₹ per reading or per litre), and outcome-based pricing (a share of savings). XaaS, everything as a service, sells the whole outcome: monitoring, analytics, maintenance and reports as a monthly service, not a box. Subscription gives predictable revenue; pay-per-use matches cost to usage; outcome-based pricing needs trusted measurement.
revenue = N × P;  cost = fixed cost + N × c;  margin = revenue − cost;  margin % = (margin ÷ revenue) × 100
blocks.where: N is the number of paying units; P is price per unit per month in ₹; c is variable cost per unit per month in ₹; fixed cost is the monthly platform or operations cost in ₹; margin is monthly profit in ₹; margin % is margin as a percentage of revenue.

blocks.text: Business processes change too. A meter reading that was a monthly visit becomes a continuous data stream. Analytics turns that stream into theft detection, demand forecasts and fault alerts. Knowledge management stores what operators learn: which fault codes repeat, which sites fail in monsoon, which thresholds cause false alarms. Value therefore sits in data and knowledge, not only in hardware.

The IoT industry is layered but not cleanly separated. A network operator may host a platform; a platform may sell an app; an integrator may own the customer relationship. Partnerships matter because no firm owns every layer. A device maker needs a certified radio; a platform needs standard APIs; an app provider needs open data models.

Standards reduce integration cost: MQTT for messaging, JSON for payloads, oneM2M for service layers, and open APIs. See Unit 3 for protocols. When standards are weak, each project is custom, margins leak into integration labour, and scaling stops at a few sites. When standards are strong, components plug in, platforms compete on analytics, and apps can move between clouds. The market shifts from selling boxes to selling uptime, insight and outcomes.

figure.caption: Monthly revenue of ₹20,00,000 splits into ₹8,75,000 of cost and ₹11,25,000 of margin. The shaded margin is 56.25% of revenue, while the platform fee of ₹5,00,000 is the largest single cost to cover.

spec.aria: A box tree: monthly revenue of ₹20,00,000 splits into total cost of ₹8,75,000 and margin of ₹11,25,000; the cost splits into ₹3,75,000 for connectivity and ₹5,00,000 for the platform.

examples.question: A smart-meter service charges ₹80 per meter per month for 25,000 meters. Platform cost is ₹5,00,000 per month, and SIM and connectivity cost is ₹15 per meter per month. Find monthly revenue, total cost and margin. Also find margin as a percentage of revenue.
steps: Connectivity cost = N × c = 25,000 × ₹15 = ₹3,75,000 per month.
Total cost = connectivity cost + platform cost = ₹3,75,000 + ₹5,00,000 = ₹8,75,000 per month.
Margin = revenue − total cost = ₹20,00,000 − ₹8,75,000 = ₹11,25,000 per month.
examples.answer: Monthly revenue is ₹20,00,000, total cost is ₹8,75,000, margin is ₹11,25,000, and margin is 56.25% of revenue.
examples.check:
n = 25000
price = 80
platform = 500000
sim = 15
revenue = n * price
conn = n * sim
total = conn + platform
margin = revenue - total
margin_pct = margin / revenue * 100
print(revenue)
print(conn)
print(total)
print(margin)
print(margin_pct)

traps: Do not equate the IoT value chain with hardware manufacturing only. Connectivity, platforms, data and services also carry value.
Do not confuse a network operator with a platform provider. One sells connectivity; the other runs device data services.
Do not compute margin percentage on cost. Use revenue as the base unless the question says otherwise.
Do not treat a one-time device sale as recurring service revenue. Subscription and pay-per-use are different models.
In M2M questions, remember the usual chain is shorter and lacks the internet-scale platform and app layers.

quiz.q: Name the six main roles shown in the IoT value chain figure.
quiz.a: Component and chip makers, device makers, network operators, platform providers, application providers, and end users. System integrators also sit between platform and customer.

quiz.q: Why can a platform provider capture more value than a device maker?
quiz.a: The platform holds device data, APIs and analytics that many apps reuse. It can earn recurring subscription revenue and scale across many device brands, while a device maker often earns a one-time sale.

quiz.q: A service has 10,000 meters at ₹100 per meter per month. Platform cost is ₹4,00,000 per month and SIM cost is ₹10 per meter per month. Find revenue, total cost, margin and margin percentage.
Why do partnerships and standards matter in a layered IoT industry?
quiz.a: No firm owns every layer. Standards such as MQTT and open APIs let devices, platforms and apps connect without custom work. Partnerships combine certified radios, connectivity, cloud and integration. Weak standards raise integration cost and block scale.

quiz.q: Distinguish subscription and pay-per-use pricing with one IoT example each.
quiz.a: Subscription charges a fixed ₹ per device per month, for example ₹80 per smart meter per month. Pay-per-use charges for actual usage, for example ₹2 per sensor reading or ₹5 per litre of water monitored.

quiz.q: A firm says it sells smart meters, so it belongs only to the device layer. Critique this view.
quiz.a: The statement confuses a product with a value chain. The meter needs connectivity, a platform and an app. Revenue may come from subscription or analytics. The firm may also act as integrator or service provider, so one label is incomplete.

quiz.q: Which roles are usually absent or weak in a simple M2M chain compared with an IoT chain?
quiz.a: M2M often lacks an internet-scale platform provider, an independent app provider, and analytics or knowledge-management services. It is more vertical and hardware-led, with direct monitoring and control.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, value-chain analysis is used to decide whether to build, buy or partner in an IoT offer. Researchers study platform economics, data ownership and outcome-based contracts. Newer curricula add digital twins and product-service systems, which extend the service layer.
